Subject: CMIzaBoPU
Text: I have compassion and love for everyone.   I understand the desire to be accepted for who you are.  However, I feel that the trans community is being used a weapon against biological women.  As a biological woman I understand the desire to be seen as having value, to be accepted for who I am, and  the desire to be treated with respect and to not be marginalized because of my gender.

Subject: CMIzaBoPU
Text: I understand that the trans community wants and deserves the same.  Unfortunately, someone has decided that the price for the recognition of the trans community had to be paid for with the degradation, humiliation and marginalization of the biological woman.

Subject: CMIzaBoPU
Text: Through conversations with younger women and some my age as well, I realized that  many of  them were not aware of just how recently women did not  have equal rights as citizens of this country.   When people think about the women's movement,  many think about the suffragette fighting for women's right to vote.   As recently as 1970, a woman could not have a credit card in her name, could not own a house, sit on a jury, or report sexual harassment in the work place.

Subject: CMIzaBoPU
Text: Married women could not make a legal contract, divorce abusive husbands, get custody of their children, and would get fired if they became pregnant.   Women were openly objectified and disrespected.

Subject: CMIzaBoPU
Text: The Equal Rights Amendment was proposed to Congress in 1923.  It was not ratified, so it was reintroduce every year for 49 years.  In 1973 congress passed the amendment and gave the states until 1979 to pass resolutions endorsing the amendment.  As of 2018, 38 states have ratified the amendment.  I was 9 years old in 1970.  When I think about the history of the women's movement, it just blows my mind that during my lifetime all that BS was still going on.

Subject: CMIzaBoPU
Text: I am writing about all of this because our stories are a huge part of our identity.

Subject: CMIzaBoPU

Subject: RcvPHgvLm
Text: @DiligentEgret That's awesome. I'll have to check it out. I do indeed use some image generators. I guess I was wondering if maybe the training for models could use more visuals to learn and then create their output--like the "black box" mystery of what happens as the model processes and then uses probability to produce its answer to your query. If it used visual processing inside there instead of trying to guess the probability of what word comes next, what might that change?

Subject: RcvPHgvLm
Text: @DiligentEgret I could be wrong, but AI can generate a lot of visual information but I don't think it yet (at least commercially/publicly) uses imagery for its own processing purposes/reasoning/probability reasoning. Integrating visual processing into AI's internal mechanisms (rather than just the text-based and numerical representations of its internal workings like it is now) could be interesting.

Subject: RKNdzyQRf
Text:
@ExcellentMantis Ai is behind facial recognition and other such tech. It is given images, told what is in them, and it learns to tell the difference when shown another image or video. Example: the training contains some dog images. It is told this is a chow, etc. It then scans an image or video and 'sees' a dog. Due to it's training, it knows what kind of dog it is and can tell you. It also knows the different colors, etc.
#AI

Subject: RcvPHgvLm
Text: @DiligentEgret I could be wrong about this too, but supposedly when AI takes in images to extract features and recognize patterns, it represents those images internally as numerical vectors, tensors, or graphs. But what doesn't currently happen is AI making decisions based on visual data without relying on text or numerical representations. So the idea is for AI to use images, scenes, or objects to represent abstract ideas for itself within its own internal mechanisms/workings.

Subject: RcvPHgvLm
Text: @DiligentEgret And to generate internal visual representations to predict outcomes or (eventually) plan actions, etc. So not just on the surface (i.e., what the model does), but underneath it--how it does it.

Subject: RKNdzyQRf
Text:
@ExcellentMantis What it does is convert the visual into data that a computer can understand. The visual information is still there even though if we, as humans, were to look at it would be meaningless. Example: This conversation would be meaningless to someone who does not understand the English language. 
#Ai

Subject: RKNdzyQRf
Text:
@ExcellentMantis It is acting as a translator by converting it's 'language' into something we can comprehend such as text or an image. I hope this makes sense. 🙂
#Ai

Subject: RcvPHgvLm
Text: @DiligentEgret Thanks, yes, that does make sense. But if AI still relies on abstract representations of visual data, rather than using the direct visual data itself as a native input for its internal decision-making processes, then I think it means it is less visually adept than it is, say, adept at language processing. So even if visual data is converted into a machine-readable format, it's still not being utilized in the same way that Large Language Models (LLMs) use text data.
